claim: Wild-type Drosophila larvae exhibit complete pupariation at 120 hr post transfer on both normal diet (ND) and protein-deprived diet (PDD).
source: At 120 hr post transfer, wild-type larvae exhibited complete pupariation on either ND or PDD, whereas itpr mutant larvae exhibited a decrease in pupariation on ND which was worsened significantly on PDD (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is directly supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1A showing pupariation percentages at 120 hr post transfer.

claim: itpr mutant larvae exhibit decreased pupariation on normal diet which is worsened significantly on protein-deprived diet.
source: At 120 hr post transfer, wild-type larvae exhibited complete pupariation on either ND or PDD, whereas itpr mutant larvae exhibited a decrease in pupariation on ND which was worsened significantly on PDD (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is directly supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1A comparing pupariation rates between wild-type and itpr mutants on different diets.

claim: Pupariation in wild-type larvae is delayed slightly when subjected to protein-deprived diet.
source: Pupariation in wild-type larvae was delayed slightly when subjected to PDD, whereas itpr mutants, which barely pupate on PDD, were delayed considerably even on a normal diet (Figure 1B,C,D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-course data shown in Figures 1B-E demonstrating the timing of pupariation under different dietary conditions.

claim: itpr mutants barely pupate on protein-deprived diet and are delayed considerably even on a normal diet.
source: Pupariation in wild-type larvae was delayed slightly when subjected to PDD, whereas itpr mutants, which barely pupate on PDD, were delayed considerably even on a normal diet (Figure 1B,C,D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-course data shown in Figures 1B-E demonstrating the timing and extent of pupariation in itpr mutants.

claim: Protein is the likely nutritional cue necessary for pupariation by itpr mutants.
source: Protein is the likely nutritional cue necessary for pupariation by itpr mutants, because the extent of pupariation on a lipid-deprived diet was significantly higher than on PDD and closer to pupariation on a normal diet (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing pupariation rates on lipid-deprived versus protein-deprived diets.

claim: Pupariation in itpr mutants is restored when the protein-deprived diet is supplemented with amino acids and vitamins.
source: Moreover, pupariation in itpr mutants was restored when the PDD was supplemented with amino acids and vitamins (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is directly supported by experimental data showing rescue of pupariation with dietary supplementation.

claim: itpr mutant larvae feed in excess of controls.
source: Interestingly, itpr mutant larvae feed in excess of controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E), but their body weights are similar to that of wild-type larvae at the time of transfer to the PDD, indicating that excess feeding may be an attempt to compensate for metabolic changes due to altered intracellular calcium signaling (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by feeding assay data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: itpr mutant larvae have body weights similar to wild-type larvae at the time of transfer to protein-deprived diet.
source: Interestingly, itpr mutant larvae feed in excess of controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E), but their body weights are similar to that of wild-type larvae at the time of transfer to the PDD, indicating that excess feeding may be an attempt to compensate for metabolic changes due to altered intracellular calcium signaling (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by weight measurement data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Excess feeding in itpr mutants may be an attempt to compensate for metabolic changes due to altered intracellular calcium signaling.
source: Interestingly, itpr mutant larvae feed in excess of controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E), but their body weights are similar to that of wild-type larvae at the time of transfer to the PDD, indicating that excess feeding may be an attempt to compensate for metabolic changes due to altered intracellular calcium signaling (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation that itpr mutants feed more but maintain similar body weight, suggesting compensatory behavior.

claim: Pan-neuronal restoration of itpr function in the mutant by expressing wild-type itpr cDNA with elav-GAL4 rescued the pupariation deficit.
source: Pan-neuronal restoration of itpr function in the mutant by expressing wild-type itpr cDNA (itpr+) with elav-GAL4 rescued the pupariation deficit, whereas pan-neuronal knockdown of the IP3R mimicked the itpr mutant phenotype on PDD, while exhibiting complete pupariation on ND (Figure 1A,B,C,D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic rescue experiments shown in Figures 1A-E.

claim: Pan-neuronal knockdown of the IP3R mimicked the itpr mutant phenotype on protein-deprived diet while exhibiting complete pupariation on normal diet.
source: Pan-neuronal restoration of itpr function in the mutant by expressing wild-type itpr cDNA (itpr+) with elav-GAL4 rescued the pupariation deficit, whereas pan-neuronal knockdown of the IP3R mimicked the itpr mutant phenotype on PDD, while exhibiting complete pupariation on ND (Figure 1A,B,C,D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAi knockdown experiments shown in Figures 1A-E.

claim: Pupariation in a protein-deprived condition requires intracellular calcium signaling through the IP3R in neurons.
source: These data demonstrate that pupariation in a protein-deprived condition requires intracellular calcium signaling through the IP3R in neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by the combined results of mutant analysis, rescue experiments, and knockdown experiments.

claim: The strongest pupariation deficit among tested neuronal subsets was observed upon IP3R knockdown in glutamatergic neurons.
source: Among the tested subsets, the strongest pupariation deficit was observed upon IP3R knockdown in glutamatergic neurons (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by a screen of IP3R knockdown in various neuronal subsets.

claim: Peptidergic neurons showed a significant pupariation deficit, but this effect was not diet specific.
source: Peptidergic neurons also showed a significant pupariation deficit, but this effect was not diet specific (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing pupariation deficits across different diets.

claim: When pan-neuronal knockdown of the IP3R was restricted to the brain lobes by introducing tsh-GAL80, pupariation was restored from less than 25% to more than 75%.
source: Interestingly, when pan-neuronal knockdown of the IP3R was restricted to the brain lobes by introducing tsh-GAL80, pupariation was restored from less than 25% (Figure 1E) to more than 75% (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic restriction experiments using GAL80.

claim: IP3R function is required to a greater extent in neurons located in the ventral ganglion for pupariation on protein-deprived diet as compared with neurons located in the central brain lobes.
source: These data indicate that IP3R function is required to a greater extent in neurons located in the ventral ganglion for pupariation on PDD as compared with neurons located in the central brain lobes.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the GAL80 restriction experiments showing differential requirements in different brain regions.

claim: VGN6341 and VGN9281-2 strains differ in their expression patterns especially in the third thoracic and initial abdominal segments of the ventral ganglion.
source: The VGN6341 and VGN9281-2 strains differ in their expression patterns especially in the third thoracic and initial abdominal segments of the ventral ganglion (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data showing expression patterns of the two GAL4 strains.

claim: IP3R knockdown with VGN6341 resulted in significantly reduced pupariation on protein-deprived diet.
source: IP3R knockdown with VGN6341 resulted in significantly reduced pupariation on PDD, whereas larvae with IP3R knockdown in VGN9281-2-expressing cells pupariated similar to control larvae (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing pupariation rates with different GAL4 drivers.

claim: Larvae with IP3R knockdown in VGN9281-2-expressing cells pupariated similar to control larvae.
source: IP3R knockdown with VGN6341 resulted in significantly reduced pupariation on PDD, whereas larvae with IP3R knockdown in VGN9281-2-expressing cells pupariated similar to control larvae (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing pupariation rates with different GAL4 drivers.

claim: Normal pupariation was observed when IP3R knockdown was restricted by introducing tsh-GAL80 in the background of VGN6341.
source: Normal pupariation was observed when IP3R knockdown was restricted by introducing tsh-GAL80 in the background of VGN6341 (referred to as restricted VGN6341; Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic restriction experiments using GAL80.

claim: tsh-GAL80 restricted expression of VGN6341 to the central brain and a few neurons in the ventral ganglion.
source: tsh-GAL80 restricted expression of VGN6341, to the central brain and a few neurons in the ventral ganglion.
evidence: The claim is supported by expression pattern analysis with GAL80.

claim: Pupariation in the itpr mutant was restored by expression of UAS-itpr+ in VGN6341 expressing neurons but not with the GAL80-restricted VGN6341 neurons.
source: In a complementary experiment, pupariation in the itpr mutant was restored by expression of UAS-itpr+ in VGN6341 expressing neurons but not with the GAL80-restricted VGN6341 neurons (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic rescue experiments.

claim: IP3R function is required in a region between the third thoracic and fifth abdominal segments in the ventral ganglion (mid-ventral ganglion or mVG) for pupariation on protein-deprived diet.
source: Comparison of VGN9281-2 and VGN6341 expression with and without tsh-GAL80 pointed to a region between the third thoracic and fifth abdominal segments in the ventral ganglion, subsequently designated as the mid-ventral ganglion or mVG, where IP3R function is required for pupariation on PDD (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is inferred from comparison of expression patterns and functional data.

claim: VGN6341-expressing cells are glutamatergic as confirmed by co-immunostaining with DvGlut.
source: These VGN6341-expressing cells were confirmed as glutamatergic by co-immunostaining of VGN6341 driven GFP with DvGlut, an established marker of glutamatergic neurons (Daniels et al., 2004) (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data and citation to established marker.

claim: DvGlut is an established marker of glutamatergic neurons.
source: These VGN6341-expressing cells were confirmed as glutamatergic by co-immunostaining of VGN6341 driven GFP with DvGlut, an established marker of glutamatergic neurons (Daniels et al., 2004) (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Twelve GPCRs were identified in the screen and validated as functioning upstream of the IP3R by rescue of pupariation with a constitutively active Gαq transgene AcGq and dSTIM.
source: Twelve GPCRs identified in the screen (Table 1) were validated as functioning upstream of the IP3R, by rescue of pupariation with two components of the IP3 signaling pathway, a constitutively active Gαq transgene AcGq and dSTIM (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic screen and rescue experiments.

claim: The muscarinic Acetylcholine Receptor (mAChR) activates Gq/PLCβ signaling leading to IP3 production and IP3-mediated Ca2+ release in Drosophila cells.
source: The mAChR activates Gq/PLCβ signaling leading to IP3 production and IP3-mediated Ca2+ release in Drosophila cells (Millar et al., 1995; Srikanth et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Knockdown of the mAChR in glutamatergic neurons of the ventral ganglion significantly reduced pupariation on protein-deficient media.
source: Knockdown of the mAChR in glutamatergic neurons of the ventral ganglion significantly reduced pupariation on protein-deficient media and expression of the mAChR+ transgene in the same neuronal subset in the itpr mutant rescued pupariation (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAi knockdown experiments.

claim: Expression of the mAChR+ transgene in glutamatergic neurons of the ventral ganglion in the itpr mutant rescued pupariation.
source: Knockdown of the mAChR in glutamatergic neurons of the ventral ganglion significantly reduced pupariation on protein-deficient media and expression of the mAChR+ transgene in the same neuronal subset in the itpr mutant rescued pupariation (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic rescue experiments.

claim: mAChR stimulation followed by Ca2+ release through the IP3R is a mechanism required by glutamatergic neurons of the mVG for pupariation under conditions of nutrient stress.
source: These data support mAChR stimulation followed by Ca2+ release through the IP3R as a mechanism required by glutamatergic neurons of the mVG for pupariation under conditions of nutrient stress.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined results of knockdown and rescue experiments.

claim: Upon stimulation with carbamylcholine (CCh), calcium transients were observed in multiple VGN6341 marked cells from larvae fed on a normal diet.
source: Upon stimulation with CCh, calcium transients were observed in multiple VGN6341 marked cells from larvae fed on a normal diet (Figure 3C,D and Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by live calcium imaging data.

claim: Pre-incubation with atropine, an established and specific antagonist of the mAChR, abolished the response to carbamylcholine.
source: The specificity of this response was ascertained by pre-incubation with atropine, an established and specific antagonist of the mAChR (Fryer and Maclagan, 1984), which abolished the response (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by pharmacological blockade experiments and citation to previous literature.

claim: Atropine is an established and specific antagonist of the mAChR.
source: The specificity of this response was ascertained by pre-incubation with atropine, an established and specific antagonist of the mAChR (Fryer and Maclagan, 1984), which abolished the response (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The response to carbamylcholine was significantly attenuated in itpr mutants on a normal diet.
source: Not surprisingly, the response to CCh was significantly attenuated in itpr mutants on a normal diet (Figure 3C,D and Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by live calcium imaging data in mutants.

claim: On protein-deprived diet, the response to carbamylcholine was reduced in neurons from control larvae, and it was nearly absent in neurons from itpr mutants.
source: On PDD, the response to CCh was reduced in neurons from control larvae, and it was nearly absent in neurons from itpr mutants (Figure 3C,E,F and G; Videos 1 and 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by live calcium imaging data comparing control and mutant responses on PDD.

claim: In control larvae, the carbamylcholine response of glutamatergic neurons reduced significantly from 2 hr to 18 hr on protein-deprived diet.
source: In control larvae, the CCh response of glutamatergic neurons reduced significantly from 2 hr to 18 hr on PDD (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-course calcium imaging data.

claim: The strongly attenuated carbamylcholine response observed in itpr mutants at 18 hr on protein-deprived diet was not evident at 2 hr on protein-deprived diet.
source: The strongly attenuated CCh response observed in itpr mutants at 18 hr on PDD was not evident at 2 hr on PDD (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-course calcium imaging data in mutants.

claim: A physiological change in the mVG glutamatergic neurons happens on protein-deprived diet over time.
source: These data indicate that a physiological change in the mVG glutamatergic neurons happens on PDD over time.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the time-dependent changes in calcium responses.

claim: The change in response to carbamylcholine over time was not evident on normal diet in either control or itpr mutant neurons.
source: The change in response to CCh over time was not evident on ND in either control or itpr mutant neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-course calcium imaging data on normal diet.

claim: The response of glutamatergic neurons in itpr mutants could be rescued by supplementing protein-deprived diet with essential amino acids.
source: Importantly, the response of glutamatergic neurons in itpr mutants could be rescued by supplementing PDD with essential amino acids (EAA) (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by dietary rescue experiments with calcium imaging.

claim: Loss of dietary essential amino acids appears to be a cause for abrogation of the carbamylcholine response in itpr mutant glutamatergic neurons after 18 hr on protein-deprived diet.
source: Thus, loss of dietary EAA appears to be a cause for abrogation of the CCh response in itpr mutant glutamatergic neurons after 18 hr on PDD.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the rescue of calcium responses by EAA supplementation.

claim: The response to carbamylcholine was absent in glutamatergic neurons of the mVG with knockdown of either mAChR or itpr on normal diet and protein-deprived diet.
source: The response to CCh was also absent in glutamatergic neurons of the mVG with knockdown of either mAChR or itpr on ND (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 2C) and PDD (Figure 3E,F,G).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data in knockdown experiments.

claim: The absence of the carbamylcholine response on normal diet in itpr and mAChR knockdowns did not correlate with a defect in pupariation.
source: The absence of the CCh response on ND in itpr and mAChR knockdowns, even though validating the original response to be through the IP3R, did not correlate with a defect in pupariation (Table 2), suggesting that mAChR and IP3R function in mVG neurons is critically required on PDD but not relevant on ND (see discussion).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of calcium imaging and pupariation data.

claim: mAChR and IP3R function in mVG neurons is critically required on protein-deprived diet but not relevant on normal diet.
source: The absence of the CCh response on ND in itpr and mAChR knockdowns, even though validating the original response to be through the IP3R, did not correlate with a defect in pupariation (Table 2), suggesting that mAChR and IP3R function in mVG neurons is critically required on PDD but not relevant on ND (see discussion).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the diet-specific effects on pupariation despite loss of calcium responses.

claim: The response to carbamylcholine on protein-deprived diet was rescued to a significant extent by over-expression of either mAChR+ or itpr+ in VGN6341-marked neurons of itpr mutants.
source: The response to CCh on PDD was rescued to a significant extent by over-expression of either mAChR+ or itpr+ in VGN6341-marked neurons of itpr mutants (Figure 3E,F and G), and correlated with rescue of pupariation observed in these genotypes (Figures 2C and 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic rescue experiments with calcium imaging.

claim: Cholinergic inputs convey protein-starvation to VGN6341-marked glutamatergic neurons possibly through acetylcholine, that activate mAChR and the IP3R for pupariation.
source: These data suggest that cholinergic inputs convey protein-starvation to VGN6341-marked glutamatergic neurons possibly through acetylcholine, that activate mAChR and the IP3R for pupariation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined results of calcium imaging, pharmacology, and genetic experiments.

claim: Pupariation was reduced significantly when cholinergic transmission was blocked by transferring larvae to the restrictive temperature for 48 hr concurrent with protein-deprivation.
source: Pupariation was reduced significantly when cholinergic transmission was blocked, by transferring larvae (80–88 hr AEL) to the restrictive temperature (29°C) for 48 hr (till 128–136 hr AEL), concurrent with protein-deprivation (Figure 3—figure supplement 2G).
evidence: The claim is supported by temperature-shift experiments blocking synaptic transmission.

claim: Normal pupariation was observed when Shits expression was driven by a combination of ChaT-GAL4 and ppk-GAL80 on the protein-deficient diet.
source: When Shits expression was driven by a combination of ChaT-GAL4 and ppk-GAL80 (blocking GAL4 activity in multidendritic sensory neurons), normal pupariation was observed on the protein-deficient diet (Figure 3—figure supplement 2G and H), suggesting the requirement of neurons expressing the Pickpocket (ppk) channel (Adams et al., 1998) in sensing protein-deficient conditions prior to pupariation.
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic restriction experiments.

claim: Neurons expressing the Pickpocket (ppk) channel are required in sensing protein-deficient conditions prior to pupariation.
source: When Shits expression was driven by a combination of ChaT-GAL4 and ppk-GAL80 (blocking GAL4 activity in multidendritic sensory neurons), normal pupariation was observed on the protein-deficient diet (Figure 3—figure supplement 2G and H), suggesting the requirement of neurons expressing the Pickpocket (ppk) channel (Adams et al., 1998) in sensing protein-deficient conditions prior to pupariation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from genetic restriction experiments and cited literature on ppk.

claim: Expression of Shits or a hyperpolarising potassium channel Kir2.1 in neurons expressing Pickpocket caused a severe pupariation deficit.
source: This idea was tested directly by expression of Shits or a hyperpolarising potassium channel Kir2.1 in neurons expressing Pickpocket (ppk-GAL4), both of which caused a severe pupariation deficit (Figure 3H, Figure 3—figure supplement 2G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experiments blocking neuronal activity.

claim: Pupariation was restored in ppk neurons with blocked activity by supplementing the protein-deficient diet with a mixture of essential amino acids.
source: Pupariation was restored in these animals by supplementing the protein-deficient diet with a mixture of EAA (Figure 3H).
evidence: The claim is supported by dietary rescue experiments.

claim: Activity in ppk-GAL4-marked neurons is required for pupariation on protein-deprived diet but not on normal diet.
source: Activity in ppk-GAL4-marked neurons is thus required for pupariation on PDD but not on ND.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the diet-specific effects of blocking ppk neuron activity.

claim: Pupariation was unaffected when activity was inhibited in cholinergic neurons marked by 19-12-GAL4 expression, which does not overlap with ppk-GAL4.
source: In contrast, pupariation was unaffected when activity was inhibited in cholinergic neurons marked by 19-12-GAL4 expression, which does not overlap with ppk-GAL4 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2G and H; Yan et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by control experiments with a different cholinergic driver and citation to previous literature.

claim: GRASP signals between VGN6341- and ppk-marked neurons were detected in the neuropil of the ventral ganglion.
source: GRASP signals between VGN6341- and ppk-marked neurons were detected in the neuropil of the ventral ganglion (Figure 3I), which is a synaptically dense region along the midline.
evidence: The claim is supported by GRASP experiments showing synaptic connectivity.

claim: The neuropil of the ventral ganglion is a synaptically dense region along the midline.
source: GRASP signals between VGN6341- and ppk-marked neurons were detected in the neuropil of the ventral ganglion (Figure 3I), which is a synaptically dense region along the midline.
evidence: The claim is based on established neuroanatomical knowledge.

claim: Calcium transients were observed in glutamatergic cells of the mVG simultaneously with optogenetic activation of cholinergic neurons on either normal diet or protein-deprived diet.
source: Calcium transients were observed in glutamatergic cells of the mVG simultaneously with optogenetic activation of cholinergic neurons on either ND or PDD (Figure 3J; Video 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by optogenetic activation experiments with calcium imaging.

claim: On protein-deprived diet, the calcium transients in glutamatergic cells appeared to oscillate upon optogenetic activation of cholinergic neurons.
source: On PDD, interestingly, the transients appeared to oscillate.
evidence: The claim is based on observation of calcium imaging data.

claim: Optogenetic activation of aminergic neurons did not elicit a response in glutamatergic neurons of the mVG.
source: As a control, we tested optogenetic activation of aminergic neurons (marked by HL9-LexA). This did not elicit a response in glutamatergic neurons of the mVG (Figure 3K).
evidence: The claim is supported by control optogenetic experiments.

claim: A robust activation of VGN6341-marked cells was observed upon optogenetic activation of ppk neurons.
source: To confirm that activation of VGN6341 neurons was through inputs from ppk neurons, we performed an optogenetic activation experiment with TrpA1-QF which marks class IV multidendritic neurons (Petersen and Stowers, 2011; subsequently referred to as ppk-QF). A robust activation of VGN6341-marked cells expressing the red shifted calcium indicator jRCaMP1b was observed upon optogenetic activation of ppk neurons expressing QUAS-ChR2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by optogenetic activation experiments with calcium imaging and citation to previous literature.

claim: Knockdown of the IP3R in cholinergic neurons did not change pupariation on protein-deprived diet.
source: Knockdown of the IP3R in cholinergic neurons did not change pupariation on PDD (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), and restoring IP3R function in cholinergic neurons failed to rescue the itpr mutant (Figure 3—figure supplement 2I).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAi knockdown and rescue experiments.

claim: Restoring IP3R function in cholinergic neurons failed to rescue the itpr mutant.
source: Knockdown of the IP3R in cholinergic neurons did not change pupariation on PDD (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), and restoring IP3R function in cholinergic neurons failed to rescue the itpr mutant (Figure 3—figure supplement 2I).
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic rescue experiments.

claim: Anterior glutamatergic projections arising from near the central mVG interneurons reach posterior projections of the mNSCs.
source: Anterior glutamatergic projections arising from near the central mVG interneurons (Figure 4A and B, arrow heads) reach posterior projections of the mNSCs (Figure 4A and B, asterisks).
evidence: The claim is supported by high-resolution imaging of neuronal projections.

claim: Anterior glutamatergic projections appear to originate from the central mVG neurons, extend laterally toward the midline for a short distance, and then project to the anterior.
source: These anterior glutamatergic projections appear to originate from the central mVG neurons, extend laterally toward the midline for a short distance, and then project to the anterior (Figure 4D and video 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by high-resolution imaging and video analysis of neuronal projections.

claim: Peripheral mVG neurons appear to project solely to the midline neuropil of the ventral ganglion.
source: They do not arise from peripheral mVG neurons that appear to project solely to the midline neuropil of the VG.
evidence: The claim is based on observation of neuronal projection patterns.

claim: A GRASP experiment between VGN6341-LexA-marked neurons and peptidergic neurons marked by dimm-GAL4 presented a complex pattern comprising medial Neurosecretory Cells (mNSCs) in the central brain, multiple projections between the mVGs and the mNSCs, and a few cell bodies and projections in the periphery of the ventral ganglion.
source: Additionally, a GRASP experiment was performed between VGN6341-LexA-marked neurons and peptidergic neurons marked by dimm-GAL4 (Figure 5A). The ensuing GRASP presented a complex pattern comprising medial Neurosecretory Cells (mNSCs) in the central brain, multiple projections between the mVGs and the mNSCs, and a few cell bodies and projections in the periphery of the ventral ganglion (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by GRASP experiments showing synaptic connectivity patterns.

claim: Pupariation was reduced significantly in animals with knockdown of the metabotropic glutamate receptor A (mGluRA) in dimm-positive neurons.
source: To test the functional significance of this apparent connectivity between peptidergic and glutamatergic cells, we measured pupariation on PDD after knockdown of various glutamatergic receptors in dimm-positive neurons. Amongst the five receptors tested, pupariation was reduced significantly in animals with knockdown of the metabotropic glutamate receptor A (mGluRA; Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAi knockdown experiments testing multiple glutamate receptors.

claim: Knockdown of mGluRA with two independent RNAi strains showed differing but significant deficits in pupariation (10% and 40%).
source: Knockdown of mGluRA with two independent RNAi strains showed differing but significant deficits in pupariation (10% and 40%; Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experiments with multiple independent RNAi lines.

claim: The difference in pupariation deficits between two mGluRA RNAi strains is attributed to the strength of the RNAi knockdown in peptidergic cells from the two different RNAi strains.
source: We attribute this difference to the strength of the RNAi knockdown in peptidergic cells from the two different RNAi strains.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the observed differences in RNAi effectiveness.

claim: Knockdown of other glutamate receptor classes resulted in normal pupariation.
source: Knockdown of other glutamate receptor classes resulted in normal pupariation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by control RNAi experiments with other glutamate receptors.

claim: Restriction of mGluRA knockdown in peptidergic neurons of the central brain and in Dilp2-positive mNSCs resulted in pupariation deficits on protein-deprived diet.
source: Restriction of mGluRA knockdown in peptidergic neurons of the central brain and in Dilp2-positive mNSCs (Dilp2-GAL4) also resulted in pupariation deficits on PDD (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic restriction experiments.

claim: Normal pupariation was observed by restricting knockdown of IP3R to VGN6341-marked glutamatergic neurons of the central brain.
source: In contrast, normal pupariation was observed by restricting knockdown of IP3R to VGN6341-marked glutamatergic neurons of the central brain (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic restriction experiments.

claim: The innervation of central brain peptidergic neurons, specifically the mNSCs, by glutamatergic neurons of the ventral ganglion appears relevant for pupariation on protein-deprived diet.
source: Taken together these data support the innervation of central brain peptidergic neurons, specifically the mNSCs, by glutamatergic neurons of the ventral ganglion. This innervation appears relevant for pupariation on PDD.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined results of GRASP, receptor knockdown, and pupariation experiments.

claim: Five of the seven Dilp2-positive cells in the mNSCs were 'GRASPed' by VGN6341.
source: Upon co-immunostaining with an antibody against Dilp2 (Géminard et al., 2009), five of the seven Dilp2-positive cells in the mNSCs were 'GRASPed' by VGN6341 (Figure 5C) as suggested earlier by immunostaining of mVG cells and the mNSCs (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by GRASP experiments with Dilp2 immunostaining and citation to antibody source.

claim: The presence of dendritic fields close to the mNSC soma has been described earlier.
source: The presence of dendritic fields close to the mNSC soma has been described earlier (Nässel et al., 2008; Vallejo et al., 2015) and was confirmed by simultaneous expression of an axonal and a dendritic marker with Dilp2-GAL4 (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature and confirmed by marker expression experiments.

claim: Axonal projections from VGN6341-marked glutamatergic neurons probably stimulate a subset of mNSCs.
source: Thus, axonal projections from VGN6341-marked glutamatergic neurons probably stimulate a subset of mNSCs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the GRASP and marker expression data.

claim: Upon optogenetic stimulation of CsChrimson in VGN6341 marked neurons, calcium transients were observed in the mNSCs of larvae from both normal and protein-deficient diets.
source: Upon optogenetic stimulation of CsChrimson in VGN6341 marked neurons calcium transients were observed in the mNSCs of larvae from both normal and protein-deficient diets (Figure 5E,F,G and H; Video 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by optogenetic activation experiments with calcium imaging.

claim: Similar activation of the mNSCs was obtained when VGN6341 marked neurons were thermogenically activated with dTrpA1.
source: Similar activation of the mNSCs was obtained when VGN6341 marked neurons were thermogenically activated with dTrpA1, a temperature-activated cation channel (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by thermogenetic activation experiments with calcium imaging.

claim: Activation of VGN6341 marked neurons in the itpr mutant did not evoke transients in mNSCs either on normal diet or on protein-deprived diet.
source: Activation of VGN6341 marked neurons in the itpr mutant, however, did not evoke transients either on ND (Figure 5E and G) or on PDD (Figure 5F and H).
evidence: The claim is supported by optogenetic activation experiments in mutants.

claim: The underlying basis for the defect in mNSC activation in itpr mutants appears to be an inability of the VGN6341-marked neurons to stimulate the mNSCs.
source: The underlying basis for this defect appears to be an inability of the VGN6341-marked neurons to stimulate the mNSCs in itpr mutants, because their optogenetic self-activation evoked robust calcium transients in itpr mutants on ND and PDD (Figure 5—figure supplement F and G).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that VGN6341 neurons themselves can be activated in mutants but cannot activate mNSCs.

claim: Activation of the Restricted VGN6341-GAL4, where GAL4 expression is absent from the mVG region, did not elicit a signal from the mNSCs.
source: Activation of the Restricted VGN6341-GAL4, where GAL4 expression is absent from the mVG region, did not elicit a signal from the mNSCs (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by control optogenetic experiments with restricted expression.

claim: Expression of dTrpA1, NaChBac, or CsChrimson in glutamatergic neurons marked by VGN6341 rescued the pupariation defect of the itpr mutant on protein-deprived diet.
source: Expression of either dTrpA1, NaChBac, or CsChrimson in glutamatergic neurons marked by VGN6341 indeed rescued the pupariation defect of the itpr mutant on PDD (Figure 5I).
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic rescue experiments using neuronal activation tools.

claim: NaChBac is a bacterial sodium channel that increases excitability of Drosophila neurons.
source: NaChBac is a bacterial sodium channel that increases excitability of Drosophila neurons (Nitabach et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Glutamatergic interneurons in the larval mVG receive cholinergic signals indicating absence of dietary amino acids, process these signals in an IP3R-dependent manner, and convey this information to peptidergic cells in the mNSCs for mounting a suitable physiological response to enable pupariation.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that glutamatergic interneurons in the larval mVG receive cholinergic signals indicating absence of dietary amino acids, process these signals in an IP3R-dependent manner, and convey this information to peptidergic cells in the mNSCs for mounting a suitable physiological response to enable pupariation.
evidence: The claim is a synthesis of multiple experimental results into a proposed circuit mechanism.

claim: Upon stimulation with 50 µM carbamylcholine, a decay in GFP fluorescence was observed in the mNSCs expressing ANF::GFP.
source: Upon stimulation with 50 µM CCh, a decay in GFP fluorescence was observed in the mNSCs (Figure 6A; Video 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging of peptide release using ANF::GFP.

claim: Application of saline did not show a change in ANF::GFP fluorescence in mNSCs.
source: Application of saline did not show a change in fluorescence (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by control experiments with saline.

claim: The extent of ANF::GFP release observed was higher in brains from larvae on protein-deprived diet as compared to larvae on normal diet.
source: The extent of release observed was higher in brains from larvae on PDD as compared to larvae on ND (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of peptide release between diets.

claim: Release of ANF::GFP was significantly attenuated in mNSCs of the itpr mutant.
source: Release of ANF::GFP was significantly attenuated in mNSCs of the itpr mutant and importantly, this could be rescued by expressing mAChR+ in glutamatergic neurons marked by VGN6341 (Figure 6B,C and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by peptide release assays in mutants.

claim: ANF::GFP release in itpr mutant mNSCs could be rescued by expressing mAChR+ in glutamatergic neurons marked by VGN6341.
source: Release of ANF::GFP was significantly attenuated in mNSCs of the itpr mutant and importantly, this could be rescued by expressing mAChR+ in glutamatergic neurons marked by VGN6341 (Figure 6B,C and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic rescue experiments with peptide release assays.

claim: Peptide release from the mNSCs was reduced significantly upon knockdown of mAChR in VGN6341-marked glutamatergic neurons.
source: Moreover, peptide release from the mNSCs was reduced significantly upon knockdown of mAChR in VGN6341-marked glutamatergic neurons and not by direct knockdown of mAChR in peptidergic neurons with dimm-GAL4 (Figure 6G).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAi knockdown experiments with peptide release assays.

claim: Peptide release from the mNSCs was not reduced by direct knockdown of mAChR in peptidergic neurons with dimm-GAL4.
source: Moreover, peptide release from the mNSCs was reduced significantly upon knockdown of mAChR in VGN6341-marked glutamatergic neurons and not by direct knockdown of mAChR in peptidergic neurons with dimm-GAL4 (Figure 6G).
evidence: The claim is supported by control RNAi experiments with peptide release assays.

claim: Cholinergic stimulation of glutamatergic neurons in the mVG appears to regulate peptide release from the mNSCs by activating mGluRA.
source: Thus, cholinergic stimulation of glutamatergic neurons in the mVG appears to regulate peptide release from the mNSCs by activating mGluRA (Figure 6G).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined results of knockdown experiments and peptide release assays.

claim: Enhanced release of ANF::GFP was observed during the period of optogenetic stimulation of VGN6341-marked glutamatergic neurons.
source: Further support for the ability of glutamatergic neurons to stimulate peptidergic release from the mNSCs comes from optogenetic stimulation of VGN6341-marked glutamatergic neurons (Figure 6D). Enhanced release of ANF::GFP was observed during the period of optogenetic stimulation (Figure 6H).
evidence: The claim is supported by optogenetic experiments with peptide release assays.

claim: Acute optogenetic inhibition of VGN6341-marked glutamatergic neurons using halorhodopsin during carbamylcholine stimulation inhibited peptide release from mNSCs.
source: Conversely, acute optogenetic inhibition of VGN6341-marked glutamatergic neurons using halorhodopsin, a light-activated chloride pump known to hyperpolarize neurons (Berni et al., 2012; Inada et al., 2011), during CCh stimulation inhibited peptide release from mNSCs (Figure 6E and I).
evidence: The claim is supported by optogenetic inhibition experiments with peptide release assays and citations to previous literature.

claim: Halorhodopsin is a light-activated chloride pump known to hyperpolarize neurons.
source: Conversely, acute optogenetic inhibition of VGN6341-marked glutamatergic neurons using halorhodopsin, a light-activated chloride pump known to hyperpolarize neurons (Berni et al., 2012; Inada et al., 2011), during CCh stimulation inhibited peptide release from mNSCs (Figure 6E and I).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In the itpr mutant, ANF::GFP release from varicosities projecting to the ring gland was significantly reduced upon stimulation with 50 µm carbachol.
source: In the itpr mutant, ANF::GFP release was significantly reduced upon stimulation with 50 µm carbachol (Figure 7A,C and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by peptide release assays from ring gland varicosities in mutants.

claim: The extent of ANF::GFP release from ring gland varicosities could be rescued by expression of mAChR+ in glutamatergic neurons marked by VGN6341.
source: The extent of release could be rescued by expression of mAChR+ in glutamatergic neurons marked by VGN6341 (Figure 7D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic rescue experiments with peptide release assays from ring gland varicosities.

claim: Similar results for ANF::GFP release were observed when expression was restricted to a subset of mNSCs marked by dilp2-GAL4.
source: Similar results were observed when expression of ANF::GFP was restricted to a subset of mNSCs marked by dilp2-GAL4 (Figure 7F–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by peptide release assays with restricted expression.

claim: Dilp2 has been implicated in the response to protein deficiency.
source: Among the peptides released from the mNSCs, Dilp2 has been implicated in the response to protein deficiency (Géminard et al., 2009; Sano et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Significant release of Dilp2 was observed post-carbamylcholine stimulation in wild-type mNSCs of larvae on normal diet and protein-deprived diet.
source: Significant release of Dilp2 was observed post-CCh stimulation, as interpreted from the reduced staining observed in wild-type mNSCs of larvae on ND and PDD (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry measuring Dilp2 levels before and after stimulation.

claim: In the itpr mutant, carbamylcholine-stimulated Dilp2 release was significantly lower, irrespective of the diets.
source: In the itpr mutant, however, CCh-stimulated Dilp2 release was significantly lower, irrespective of the diets (Figure 8A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry measuring Dilp2 release in mutants.

claim: Carbamylcholine stimulation of brains with itpr knockdown in neurons marked by VGN6341 induced weaker release of Dilp2.
source: CCh stimulation of brains with itpr knockdown in neurons marked by VGN6341 also induced weaker release of Dilp2 (Figure 8C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry in knockdown experiments.

claim: When Dilp2+ was over-expressed using Dilp2-GAL4, a partial rescue of pupariation in the itpr mutant was observed on protein-deprived diet.
source: Taking these observations forward, when Dilp2+was over-expressed using Dilp2-GAL4, or when Dilp2 positive neurons were maintained in an excitable state by expression of NaChBac, a partial rescue of pupariation in the itpr mutant was observed on PDD (Figure 8D).
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic rescue experiments.

claim: When Dilp2 positive neurons were maintained in an excitable state by expression of NaChBac, a partial rescue of pupariation in the itpr mutant was observed on protein-deprived diet.
source: Taking these observations forward, when Dilp2+was over-expressed using Dilp2-GAL4, or when Dilp2 positive neurons were maintained in an excitable state by expression of NaChBac, a partial rescue of pupariation in the itpr mutant was observed on PDD (Figure 8D).
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic rescue experiments.

claim: Pupariation on a protein-deficient diet requires mVG-mediated neuropeptide release from the mNSCs.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that pupariation on a protein-deficient diet requires mVG-mediated neuropeptide release from the mNSCs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined results of peptide release and pupariation experiments.

claim: Higher levels of Dilp2 were observed in the larval mNSCs of IP3R mutants.
source: Higher levels of Dilp2 were observed in the larval mNSCs of IP3R mutants, as well as in larvae with IP3R knockdown in glutamatergic neurons of the ventral ganglion.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data.

claim: Higher levels of Dilp2 were observed in larvae with IP3R knockdown in glutamatergic neurons of the ventral ganglion.
source: Higher levels of Dilp2 were observed in the larval mNSCs of IP3R mutants, as well as in larvae with IP3R knockdown in glutamatergic neurons of the ventral ganglion.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data.

claim: The excess Dilp2 in IP3R mutants is attributed to reduced release of Dilp2 from the mNSCs.
source: We attribute the excess Dilp2 to reduced release of Dilp2 from the mNSCs.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the observed accumulation of Dilp2.

claim: The absence of up-regulation of dilp2 transcripts in IP3R mutants supports the idea that excess Dilp2 is due to reduced release.
source: The absence of up-regulation of dilp2 transcripts in IP3R mutants supports this idea (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data showing no change in dilp2 mRNA levels.

claim: This is the first report of Dilp2 regulation by neurons in the ventral ganglion.
source: This is, to our knowledge, the first report of Dilp2 regulation by neurons in the ventral ganglion.
evidence: The claim is a statement of novelty based on the authors' knowledge of the literature.

claim: Environmental nutrients regulating Dilp function has been well documented.
source: Environmental nutrients regulating Dilp function has been well documented (Géminard et al., 2009; Kim and Neufeld, 2015; Rajan and Perrimon, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Most studies on Dilp regulation report remote sensing attributed to the fat body.
source: Most of these studies report remote sensing attributed to the fat body (Géminard et al., 2009; Koyama and Mirth, 2016; Rajan and Perrimon, 2012; Sano et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The regulation of Dilp2 by ventral ganglion neurons is another layer in the overall regulation of Dilps in Drosophila that seems to be particularly important upon protein-deprivation.
source: The regulation we report here is another layer in the overall regulation of Dilps in Drosophila that seems to be particularly important upon protein-deprivation.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the findings in the context of existing knowledge.

claim: A peak of ecdysone release late in the wandering third-instar triggers larval pupariation on normal diet.
source: A peak of ecdysone release late in the wandering third-instar triggers larval pupariation on ND (Warren et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Expression levels of genes encoding enzymes of the ecdysteroid biosynthetic pathway have been studied in larvae on a normal diet.
source: Expression levels of genes encoding enzymes of the ecdysteroid biosynthetic pathway have been studied (McBrayer et al., 2007; Shimada-Niwa and Niwa, 2014), in larvae on a normal diet.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Transcripts of shadow, spookier, phantom, neverland and disembodied are up-regulated dramatically before pupariation.
source: Specifically, transcripts of shadow (sad), spookier (spok), phantom (phm), neverland (nvd) and disembodied (dib) are up-regulated dramatically before pupariation (McBrayer et al., 2007; Shimada-Niwa and Niwa, 2014; Warren et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The neural circuit identified for pupariation on protein-deprived diet likely affects ecdysone synthesis by regulating ecdysteroid biosynthesis.
source: It is therefore likely that the neural circuit identified for pupariation on PDD affects ecdysone synthesis by regulating ecdysteroid biosynthesis.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the known role of ecdysone in pupariation and the circuit's effect on pupariation.

claim: Transcripts for shadow, spookier, phantom, neverland and disembodied peaked approximately 42 hr post protein-deprivation in wild-type larvae aged 80–88 hr AEL.
source: Transcripts for all these genes peaked approximately 42 hr post protein-deprivation in wild-type larvae aged 80–88 hr AEL (Figure 9A).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR time-course data.

claim: The expression levels of ecdysteroid biosynthetic genes were lower in the itpr mutant at 42 hr and 66 hr post protein-deprivation.
source: The expression levels of these genes were lower in the itpr mutant at 42 hr and 66 hr and could be significantly rescued by overexpression of mAChR+in the neurons marked by VGN6341, especially at 66 hr (Figure 9B).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data in mutants.

claim: Expression levels of ecdysteroid biosynthetic genes could be significantly rescued by overexpression of mAChR+ in the neurons marked by VGN6341, especially at 66 hr.
source: The expression levels of these genes were lower in the itpr mutant at 42 hr and 66 hr and could be significantly rescued by overexpression of mAChR+in the neurons marked by VGN6341, especially at 66 hr (Figure 9B).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data in rescue experiments.

claim: Up-regulation of ecdysteroid biosynthetic genes corresponded to a rescue in pupariation.
source: Their up-regulation corresponded to a rescue in pupariation as well (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation between gene expression and pupariation data.

claim: Glutamatergic neurons of the mVG regulate expression of genes required for the ecdysone peak for pupariation on protein-deprived diet in a mAChR- and itpr-dependent manner.
source: Taken together these data indicate that glutamatergic neurons of the mVG regulate expression of genes required for the ecdysone peak for pupariation on PDD in a mAChR- and itpr-dependent manner (Figure 9C and D).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined results of gene expression, rescue, and pupariation experiments.

claim: Ecdysteroid synthesis and release is regulated by neuropeptides, predominantly prothoracicotropic hormone (PTTH).
source: Ecdysteroid synthesis and release is regulated by neuropeptides, predominantly prothoracicotropic hormone (PTTH) (McBrayer et al., 2007; Mirth et al., 2005), as well as through insulin signaling (Colombani et al., 2005; Mirth et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Ecdysteroid synthesis and release is regulated through insulin signaling.
source: Ecdysteroid synthesis and release is regulated by neuropeptides, predominantly prothoracicotropic hormone (PTTH) (McBrayer et al., 2007; Mirth et al., 2005), as well as through insulin signaling (Colombani et al., 2005; Mirth et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The regulation of ecdysone synthesis by the mVG is through neuropeptide release from the mNSCs.
source: We propose that this regulation of ecdysone synthesis by the mVG is through neuropeptide release from the mNSCs.
evidence: The claim is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental findings.

claim: Protein-deprivation signals are sensed by Pickpocket-expressing sensory neurons and conveyed to glutamatergic interneurons of the mid-ventral ganglion.
source: In this study, we demonstrate that protein-deprivation signals are sensed by Pickpocket-expressing sensory neurons and conveyed to glutamatergic interneurons of the mid-ventral ganglion (mVG).
evidence: The claim is a summary of the main findings from multiple experiments.

claim: mVG glutamatergic neurons require mAChR-stimulated intracellular Ca2+ release through the IP3R to signal to downstream peptidergic neurons, including the medial neurosecretory cells.
source: These mVG neurons require mAChR-stimulated intracellular Ca2+ release through the IP3R to signal to downstream peptidergic neurons, including the medial neurosecretory cells.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the main findings from multiple experiments.

claim: On a protein-deficient diet, connections between mVG neurons and mNSCs stimulate release of neuropeptides, which in turn, regulate expression of genes required for ecdysteroid biosynthesis to allow pupariation.
source: On a protein-deficient diet, these connections stimulate release of neuropeptides, which in turn, regulate expression of genes required for ecdysteroid biosynthesis to allow pupariation (Figure 9D).
evidence: The claim is a summary of the main findings from multiple experiments.

claim: Calcium responses of mVG glutamatergic neurons differ between the normal and protein-deficient diets.
source: Calcium responses of mVG glutamatergic neurons differ between the normal and protein-deficient diets, suggesting that nutrient-dependent changes take place in these neurons that affect their cellular signaling properties.
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data comparing responses on different diets.

claim: Nutrient-dependent changes take place in mVG glutamatergic neurons that affect their cellular signaling properties.
source: Calcium responses of mVG glutamatergic neurons differ between the normal and protein-deficient diets, suggesting that nutrient-dependent changes take place in these neurons that affect their cellular signaling properties.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observed differences in calcium responses.

claim: Knockdown of either mAChR or itpr in the mVG neurons blocks the functional connectivity between these neurons and the mNSCs.
source: Knockdown of either mAChR or itpr in the mVG neurons blocks the functional connectivity between these neurons and the mNSCs (Figure 9C).
evidence: The claim is supported by optogenetic and calcium imaging experiments in knockdown conditions.

claim: The loss of connectivity between mVG neurons and mNSCs affects neuropeptide release from the mNSCs that is required for pupariation under protein-deprivation.
source: The loss of this connectivity affects neuropeptide release from the mNSCs that is required for pupariation under protein-deprivation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined results of connectivity, peptide release, and pupariation experiments.

claim: Glutamatergic signals from the mVG are apparently not essential for pupariation on a normal diet.
source: Glutamatergic signals from the mVG are apparently not essential for pupariation on a normal diet, indicating that the likely function of this circuit is an adaptation to uncertain availability of food in nature.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the diet-specific effects observed in the experiments.

claim: The likely function of the mVG glutamatergic circuit is an adaptation to uncertain availability of food in nature.
source: Glutamatergic signals from the mVG are apparently not essential for pupariation on a normal diet, indicating that the likely function of this circuit is an adaptation to uncertain availability of food in nature.
evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation of the circuit's evolutionary function.

claim: The Drosophila larval nervous system consists of approximately 10,000 neurons.
source: A less-complex nervous system, consisting of approximately 10,000 neurons (Scott et al., 2001), compared with 70 million neurons in the mouse brain (Economo et al., 2016), makes Drosophila larvae a powerful system to elucidate central brain circuitry underlying systemic responses to nutrient deprivation (Bjordal et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The mouse brain contains 70 million neurons.
source: A less-complex nervous system, consisting of approximately 10,000 neurons (Scott et al., 2001), compared with 70 million neurons in the mouse brain (Economo et al., 2016), makes Drosophila larvae a powerful system to elucidate central brain circuitry underlying systemic responses to nutrient deprivation (Bjordal et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Drosophila larvae are a powerful system to elucidate central brain circuitry underlying systemic responses to nutrient deprivation.
source: A less-complex nervous system, consisting of approximately 10,000 neurons (Scott et al., 2001), compared with 70 million neurons in the mouse brain (Economo et al., 2016), makes Drosophila larvae a powerful system to elucidate central brain circuitry underlying systemic responses to nutrient deprivation (Bjordal et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature and the comparative simplicity of the Drosophila nervous system.

claim: IP3R is encoded by the single itpr gene in Drosophila.
source: In Drosophila, IP3R is encoded by the single itpr gene (Hasan and Rosbash, 1992).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: IP3R mutants exhibit delayed moulting.
source: IP3R mutants exhibit delayed moulting (Venkatesh and Hasan, 1997) recently attributed to release of the steroid hormone ecdysone from the prothoracic gland (Yamanaka et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Delayed moulting in IP3R mutants is recently attributed to release of the steroid hormone ecdysone from the prothoracic gland.
source: IP3R mutants exhibit delayed moulting (Venkatesh and Hasan, 1997) recently attributed to release of the steroid hormone ecdysone from the prothoracic gland (Yamanaka et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Null alleles of itpr are lethal as second instar larvae.
source: While null alleles are lethal as second instar larvae, heteroallelic hypomorphs exhibit developmental and metabolic phenotypes.
evidence: The claim is based on established genetic knowledge of itpr alleles.

claim: Heteroallelic hypomorphs of itpr exhibit developmental and metabolic phenotypes ranging from lethality across larval stages to hyperphagic adults with altered lipid metabolism.
source: While null alleles are lethal as second instar larvae, heteroallelic hypomorphs exhibit developmental and metabolic phenotypes. These range from lethality across larval stages to hyperphagic adults with altered lipid metabolism.
evidence: The claim is based on established genetic knowledge of itpr alleles.

claim: The focus of adult metabolic defects observed in itpr mutants appears to be the central nervous system.
source: The focus of adult metabolic defects observed in itpr mutants appears to be the central nervous system (Subramanian et al., 2013a, 2013b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The Drosophila larval to pupal transition requires systemic integration of the nutritional state of late-stage larvae with release of hormones that drive pupariation.
source: This transition requires systemic integration of the nutritional state of late-stage larvae with release of hormones that drive pupariation (Andersen et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Oscillations in calcium are known to cause exocytosis of neuropeptides.
source: Such oscillations are known to cause exocytosis of neuropeptides (Tse et al., 1993) and may underlie enhanced neuropeptide secretion required for pupariation on PDD.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Oscillations in calcium may underlie enhanced neuropeptide secretion required for pupariation on protein-deprived diet.
source: Such oscillations are known to cause exocytosis of neuropeptides (Tse et al., 1993) and may underlie enhanced neuropeptide secretion required for pupariation on PDD.
evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation based on known mechanisms and observed oscillations.

claim: Dopaminergic neurons in the larval brain of Drosophila directly sense amino acids leading to their activation and consequent changes in food-intake behaviour on an amino acid deficient medium.
source: In a recent report, dopaminergic neurons in the larval brain of Drosophila were demonstrated as directly sensing amino acids leading to their activation and consequent changes in food-intake behaviour on an amino acid deficient medium (Bjordal et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The findings on dopaminergic amino acid sensing do not explain the full range of responses to amino acid deprivation.
source: These findings, however, do not explain the full range of responses to amino acid deprivation.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the limitations of previous work.
